en: The Path of Discrimination,
Chapter on Wisdom, 3.9.
Discourse on Insight (Vipassanā)
Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Monks,” [he said].
“Venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One spoke as follows:
“Bhikkhus, it is impossible that a bhikkhu who regards any conditioned phenomenon as permanent will possess the conformity-acceptance;
and it is impossible that one who does not possess the conformity-acceptance will enter the fixed course of rightness.”
This is impossible:
that one who does not enter the certainty of rightness will realize the fruit of stream-entry, or the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning,
or arhatship— this is impossible.
"Indeed, monks, it is possible that a bhikkhu who contemplates all conditioned phenomena as impermanent will possess the conformable acceptance;
and it is possible that one possessing the conformable acceptance will enter the certainty of rightness."
"It is possible that, entering the fixed course of rightness, he will realize the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, or arhatship—
it is indeed possible. But, monks,
for a bhikkhu who regards any conditioned phenomenon as pleasant, it is impossible that he will possess the acceptance that is in conformity [with the truth]."
It is impossible that this should happen:
that one who lacks the conformable acceptance will enter the fixed course of rightness;
it is impossible that this should happen.

"It is impossible that one who has not entered the certainty of rightness will realize the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, or arahantship— this cannot be.
But it is possible, monks,
that a monk who regards all conditioned phenomena as suffering will possess the conformity-acceptance."
It is possible that one who possesses conformity-acceptance will enter the fixed course of rightness—
it is possible.
"It is possible that a monk who is entering the fixed course of rightness will realize the fruit of stream-entry, or the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning, or even arhatship—
this is a possibility. But, monks,
it is impossible that a monk who regards any phenomenon as a self will possess the conformable patience."
It is impossible that this could happen:
that one who lacks the conformable acceptance (anulomikā khanti) would enter the fixed course of rightness (sammattaniyāma);
it is impossible that this could happen.
"It is impossible that one who has not entered the certainty of rightness will realize the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, or arahantship—
this cannot happen. Indeed, monks, it is possible that a monk who contemplates all phenomena as non-self will come to possess the conformable patience."
It is possible that one who possesses conformity-acceptance will enter the fixed course of rightness—
it is possible.
"It is possible that one who enters the certainty of rightness will realize the fruit of stream-entry, or the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning, or even arhatship—
this is a possibility. But, monks, how could that bhikkhu— who perceives Nibbāna as suffering— ever possess the conformable patience?"
It is impossible that this could happen:
that one who lacks the conformable acceptance (anulomikā khanti) would enter the fixed course of rightness (sammattaniyāma).
It is impossible that this could happen.
"It is impossible, monks, that one who has not entered the certainty of rightness will realize the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, or arahantship—
this is not possible. Indeed, monks, it is impossible that a monk who regards Nibbāna as happiness will be possessed of the conformable patience."
It is possible that one who possesses conformity-acceptance will enter into the certainty of rightness—
it is possible.

"It is possible that one who is entering the certainty of rightness (sammattaniyāma) will realize the fruit of stream-entry, or the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning, or even arhatship—this is a possibility.
In how many ways does one acquire the conformable acceptance (anulomika-khanti)? In how many ways does one enter the certainty of rightness?
One acquires conformity-acceptance through forty modes; one enters the certainty of rightness through forty modes.
What are the forty modes through which one acquires conformity-acceptance? What are the forty modes through which one enters the certainty of rightness?
[By viewing] the five aggregates as impermanent, as suffering, as a disease, as a tumor, as a dart, as a calamity, as an affliction, as alien, as disintegrating...
From pestilence, from calamity, from fear, from misfortune, from instability, from perishability, from impermanence,

from lack of refuge, from lack of shelter, from lack of protection, from emptiness, from vanity, from voidness, from selflessness, from danger, from the nature of change, from worthlessness, from the root of evil,
from being a murderer, from dissolution, from being subject to taints, from being conditioned, from being the bait of Māra, and from the nature of birth, aging, and sickness.
One who views the five aggregates as subject to death, subject to sorrow, subject to lamentation, subject to despair, and subject to defilement,
acquires the conformable patience (*anulomikā khanti*).
One who views the cessation of the five aggregates as the permanent Nibbāna enters the fixed course of rightness (*sammattaniyāma*).
Seeing the five aggregates as suffering, one acquires conformity-patience.
Seeing the cessation of the five aggregates as blissful Nibbāna, one enters the certainty of rightness.
Seeing the five aggregates as a disease, one acquires conformity-patience.
Seeing the cessation of the five aggregates as health and Nibbāna, one enters the certainty of rightness (*sammattaniyāma*).
Seeing the five aggregates as a tumor, one acquires the conformable acceptance (*anulomikā khanti*).
Seeing the cessation of the five aggregates as the tumor-free Nibbāna, one enters the certainty of rightness.
Seeing the five aggregates as a dart, one acquires conformity-acceptance (*anulomikā khanti*).
Seeing the cessation of the five aggregates as the dartless Nibbāna, one enters the certainty of rightness (*sammattaniyāma*).
Seeing the five aggregates as misery, one acquires conformity-acceptance.
Seeing the cessation of the five aggregates as the blameless Nibbāna, one enters the fixed course of rightness (*sammattaniyāma*).
Seeing the five aggregates as a disease, one acquires the conformable acceptance (*anulomikā khanti*).
Seeing the cessation of the five aggregates as the health of Nibbāna, one enters the fixed course of rightness.
Seeing the five aggregates as alien, one acquires conformity-acceptance (*anulomikā khanti*).
Seeing the cessation of the five aggregates as Nibbāna, which is not dependent on another, one enters the certainty of rightness (*sammattaniyāma*).
Seeing the five aggregates as disintegrating, one acquires conformity-acceptance.
Seeing the cessation of the five aggregates as the nature of illumination, Nibbāna, one enters the certainty of rightness.
Seeing the five aggregates as a plague, one acquires the conformable patience.
Seeing the cessation of the five aggregates as the plague-free Nibbāna, one enters the certainty of rightness.
Seeing the five aggregates as a calamity, one acquires conformity-acceptance (*anulomikā khanti*).
Seeing the cessation of the five aggregates as the security of Nibbāna, one enters the certainty of rightness (*sammattaniyāma*).
Seeing the five aggregates as a danger, one acquires conformity-acceptance.
Seeing the cessation of the five aggregates as the fearless Nibbāna, one enters the fixed course of rightness (*sammattaniyāma*).
Seeing the five aggregates as affliction (*upasagga*), one acquires the conformable acceptance (*anulomikā khanti*).
Seeing the cessation of the five aggregates as the unafflicted Nibbāna, one enters the fixed course of rightness.
Contemplating the five aggregates as moving, one attains conformity-acceptance (*anulomikā khanti*).
Contemplating the cessation of the five aggregates as the immovable Nibbāna, one enters the certainty of rightness (*sammattaniyāma*).
Contemplating the five aggregates as subject to dissolution, one attains conformity-acceptance.
Seeing the cessation of the five aggregates as the indestructible Nibbāna, one enters the certainty of rightness.
Seeing the five aggregates as impermanent, one acquires the conformable patience.
Seeing the cessation of the five aggregates as the permanent Nibbāna, one enters the certainty of rightness.
Seeing the five aggregates as providing no protection, one acquires conformity-acceptance (*anulomikā khanti*).
Seeing the cessation of the five aggregates as protection—namely, Nibbāna—one enters the certainty of rightness (*sammattaniyāma*).
Seeing the five aggregates as providing no refuge, one acquires conformity-acceptance.
Seeing the cessation of the five aggregates as a refuge and Nibbāna, one enters the certainty of rightness.
Seeing the five aggregates as a non-refuge, one acquires the conformable acceptance.
Seeing the cessation of the five aggregates as a refuge and Nibbāna, one enters the certainty of rightness.
One who perceives the five aggregates as empty attains conformity-patience.
One who perceives the cessation of the five aggregates as the non-empty Nibbāna enters the fixed course of rightness.
One who perceives the five aggregates as vain attains conformity-patience.
Seeing the cessation of the five aggregates as non-vacuous Nibbāna, one enters the certainty of rightness.
Seeing the five aggregates as empty, one acquires the conformable acceptance.
Seeing the cessation of the five aggregates as the supreme emptiness of Nibbāna, one enters the certainty of rightness.
Seeing the five aggregates as non-self, one acquires conformity-acceptance (*anulomikā khanti*).
Seeing the cessation of the five aggregates as the ultimate Nibbāna, one enters the certainty of rightness (*sammattaniyāma*).
Seeing the five aggregates as fraught with danger, one acquires conformity-acceptance.
Seeing the cessation of the five aggregates as the faultless Nibbāna, one enters the certainty of rightness (*sammattaniyāma*).
Seeing the five aggregates as subject to change, one acquires the conformable acceptance (*anulomikā khanti*).
Seeing the cessation of the five aggregates as the unchanging Nibbāna, one enters the certainty of rightness.
Seeing the five aggregates as being without essence, one attains conformity-acceptance (*anulomikā khanti*).
Seeing the cessation of the five aggregates as the essence, Nibbāna, one enters the certainty of rightness (*sammattaniyāma*).
Seeing the five aggregates as the root of suffering, one attains conformity-acceptance.
Seeing the cessation of the five aggregates as Nibbāna, the root of the blameless, one enters the fixed course of rightness.
Seeing the five aggregates as murderers, one acquires the conformity-acceptance (*anulomikā khanti*).
Seeing the cessation of the five aggregates as the non-murderous Nibbāna, one enters the fixed course of rightness.
Seeing the five aggregates as subject to dissolution, one acquires conformity-acceptance (*anulomikā khanti*).
Seeing the cessation of the five aggregates as non-dissolution, that is, Nibbāna, one enters the certainty of rightness (*sammattaniyāma*).
Seeing the five aggregates as accompanied by taints (*sāsavato*), one acquires conformity-acceptance.
Seeing the cessation of the five aggregates as the untainted Nibbāna, one enters the certainty of rightness.
Seeing the five aggregates as conditioned, one acquires the conformable acceptance.
Seeing the cessation of the five aggregates as the unconditioned Nibbāna, one enters the certainty of rightness.
Seeing the five aggregates as the bait of Māra, one attains conformity-patience (*anulomikā khanti*).
Seeing the cessation of the five aggregates as the unworldly Nibbāna, one enters the certainty of rightness (*sammattaniyāma*).
Seeing the five aggregates as subject to birth, one attains conformity-patience.
Seeing the cessation of the five aggregates as the unborn Nibbāna, one enters the fixed course of rightness.
Seeing the five aggregates as subject to aging, one acquires the conformable patience.
Seeing the cessation of the five aggregates as the ageless Nibbāna, one enters the fixed course of rightness.
Seeing the five aggregates as subject to the nature of disease, one attains conformity-acceptance (*anulomikā khanti*).
Seeing the cessation of the five aggregates as non-disease, Nibbāna, one enters the fixed course of rightness (*sammattaniyāma*).
Seeing the five aggregates as subject to the nature of death, one attains conformity-acceptance.
Seeing the cessation of the five aggregates as the deathless Nibbāna, one enters the certainty of rightness.
Seeing the five aggregates as subject to sorrow, one attains the conformable acceptance.
Seeing the cessation of the five aggregates as sorrowless Nibbāna, one enters the certainty of rightness.
Contemplating the five aggregates as subject to lamentation, one acquires conformity-patience.
Contemplating the cessation of the five aggregates as the lamentation-free Nibbāna, one enters the fixed course of rightness.
Contemplating the five aggregates as subject to despair, one acquires conformity-patience.
Seeing the cessation of the five aggregates as Nibbāna, which is free from distress, one enters the fixed course of rightness.
Seeing the five aggregates as phenomena subject to defilement, one acquires the conformable acceptance.
Seeing the cessation of the five aggregates as Nibbāna, which is undefiled, one enters the fixed course of rightness.
"As impermanent" means the contemplation of impermanence.
"As suffering" means the contemplation of suffering.
"As a disease" means the contemplation of suffering.
As a tumor, it is the contemplation of suffering.
As an arrow, it is the contemplation of suffering.
As misery, it is the contemplation of suffering.
"As affliction" is contemplation of suffering.
"As alien" is contemplation of non-self.
"As disintegration" is contemplation of impermanence.
As "misfortune," it is the contemplation of suffering.
As "calamity," it is the contemplation of suffering.
As "terror," it is the contemplation of suffering.
"From oppression" refers to the contemplation of suffering.
"From wavering" refers to the contemplation of impermanence.
"From disintegration" refers to the contemplation of impermanence.
"Addhuvato" means contemplation of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*).
"Atāṇato" means contemplation of suffering (*dukkhānupassanā*).
"Aleṇato" means contemplation of suffering (*dukkhānupassanā*).
"As shelterless" refers to the contemplation of suffering.
"As empty" refers to the contemplation of non-self.
"As vain" refers to the contemplation of non-self.
"By way of emptiness" means contemplation of non-self.
"By way of non-self" means contemplation of non-self.
"By way of danger" means contemplation of suffering.
"Subject to change" refers to the contemplation of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*).
"Lacking essence" refers to the contemplation of non-self (*anattānupassanā*).
"The root of suffering" refers to the contemplation of suffering (*dukkhānupassanā*).
"As a murderer" refers to the contemplation of suffering.
"As subject to dissolution" refers to the contemplation of impermanence.
"As accompanied by taints" refers to the contemplation of suffering.
"Conditioned" refers to the contemplation of impermanence.
"The bait of Māra" refers to the contemplation of suffering.
"Subject to birth" refers to the contemplation of suffering.
"Subject to aging" is the contemplation of suffering.
"Subject to illness" is the contemplation of suffering.
"Subject to death" is the contemplation of impermanence.
"Subject to sorrow" is contemplation of suffering.
"Subject to lamentation" is contemplation of suffering.
"Subject to despair" is contemplation of suffering.
"By way of phenomena subject to defilement" refers to the contemplation of suffering.
Through these forty aspects, one attains conformity-acceptance (*anulomika-khanti*).
Through these forty aspects, one enters the certainty of rightness (*sammattaniyāma*).
For one who attains conformity-acceptance through these forty aspects, and for one who enters the certainty of rightness through these forty aspects,
how many are contemplations of impermanence, how many are contemplations of suffering, and how many are contemplations of non-self?
Twenty-five are contemplations of non-self.
There are fifty contemplations on impermanence,
and exactly twenty-five that are said to pertain to suffering.
The Discussion on Insight is finished.
